comparator.name: Bachelor Gezondheidswetenschappen, Beleid & Management Gezondheidszorg
comparator.sourceNotes: UNFINISHED EXTERNAL VERIFICATION: the stored 11-component 180-EC accounting (eight 15-EC blocks, 25-EC free choice, 15-EC Choices and Dilemmas and 20-EC graduation) is preserved provisionally, not certified. The current programme page states 30 EC free choice; indexed text of the linked 2026–2027 OER states 25 EC. Visual inspection of the actual PDF, its visible/hidden text and current edition is required to resolve this material discrepancy and check all module/PPO and progression conditions. Direct downloads, search PDF rendering and browser retrieval currently fail with connection timeouts. No credit redistribution is inferred. Current official pages establish the Dutch full-time BSc identity, 180 EC overall, eight first/two-year themes, applied multidisciplinary health-services enquiry and placement-based independent research. The audience view is unresolved and withholds all purported complete curricula and UCR comparisons until the source conflict and remaining gates are resolved.
components: Open year-three space that may be completed through an approved minor, electives, exchange or international placement.
Placement-based independent research comprising responsibility for the problem statement, design, fieldwork and report.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Healthcare systems, policy, governance, law and public decision-making
Health economics, affordability, insurance, markets and allocation
Healthcare organisations, management, quality and stakeholder coordination
Public health, epidemiology, prevention and social-medical perspectives on health and illness
Health behaviour, medical sociology, inequality, culture and stigma
Qualitative and quantitative healthcare research, evidence assessment and academic communication
Ethical dilemmas and interdisciplinary choices in healthcare
Independent applied health research in an organisational setting
adjacent: Ageing, lifecourse needs and future care
Youth care, mental healthcare and welfare
questions: How should government, markets and insurance organise accessible and affordable healthcare?
How do governments, insurers, organisations, professionals and patients interact in healthcare?
How can complex health problems be analysed and addressed across social, behavioural, legal, economic and organisational perspectives?

candidates.label: Healthcare markets, insurance and organisational governance

selection.assessment: Two provisional programmes survive the course-content challenge. The original markets option had no health course and depended on relabelling generic economics, global business and leadership as healthcare teaching. Adding the necessary health-science anchor and retaining relevant economic/organisational tools converges on the closest programme; residual business specialisation does not establish a substantively distinct healthcare-markets curriculum. The lifecourse option sustains actual health/developmental content and differs meaningfully from the closest. A separate healthcare-innovation programme is not established by generic business innovation or technical/image-analysis courses: these do not teach the external organisational implementation and service-design enquiry. Its clinical-AI ethics aspect is retained in both programmes, without claiming a full innovation-design route. No third option is manufactured. Final endorsement remains pending resolution of the external curriculum credit conflict.

alternatives.label: Population health, institutions & society
alternatives.labelReason: Actual health and population study anchors the programme; institutional and organisational analysis is complementary. The label avoids claiming a specialist healthcare-policy or healthcare-management degree.
alternatives.concept: A population-health programme combines epidemiology, medical and health psychology, lifespan development and disease mechanisms with statistics, qualitative research and research synthesis. Economics, accounting, organisational psychology, public institutions, rights and ethics provide complementary tools for understanding collective choices and organisations. AI Ethics directly considers confidentiality, responsibility and trust in clinical and therapeutic settings. The programme sustains study of health and illness; its general legal, economic and management courses do not become Dutch health-system, health-insurance or patient-law training.
progression: Semester 1 establishes epidemiology, economics, law and sociology; semester 2 adds PPD, general research/statistics, brain/behaviour and qualitative methods. Semester 3 introduces biological foundations, multivariate statistics, human rights and comparative politics. Semester 4 adds economics, lifespan development and evidence synthesis. Semester 5 combines health psychology, organisations, accounting and social theory. The final semester adds econometrics, ethics, mechanisms of disease and AI ethics. The biological gateway precedes disease mechanisms, the psychology gateway precedes dependent psychology, and the methods gateway precedes dependent economics/organisational courses. Every assigned offering and formal prerequisite is independently checked.

alternatives.label: Lifecourse health & society
alternatives.labelReason: The actual composition supports health needs, psychological development and society across the lifecourse. It does not imply delivery of mental healthcare or professional qualification.
alternatives.concept: This health-and-society programme centres epidemiology, health and abnormal psychology, lifespan development, youth resilience, psychological assessment concepts and research synthesis. Sociology, qualitative methods, public economics, organisations, rights and ethics support inquiry into health needs, social conditions and collective choices. AI Ethics adds a direct examination of clinical confidentiality and children’s interactions with AI. Psychological assessment and psychotherapy are studied academically; the programme does not provide clinical care training or the external degree’s integrated youth-service and healthcare-policy practice.
alternatives.distinctness: The programmes share 18 courses, with 6 different courses (45 EC) in each. The closest adds biological/disease science, accounting, microeconomics and econometrics; the related programme adds social and abnormal psychology, youth resilience, assessment/psychotherapy concepts, modern sociology and constitutional comparison. Their organising questions differ between population/institutional analysis and development, mental health and social conditions across the lifecourse.
progression: Semester 1 starts with PPD, epidemiology, law and sociology. Semester 2 introduces brain/behaviour, general research/statistics, social psychology and AI ethics; semester 3 adds multivariate statistics, rights, comparative politics and social theory. Semester 4 studies abnormal psychology, lifespan development, public economics and constitutional comparison. Semester 5 studies health psychology, youth resilience, contemporary social theory and organisations. The final semester combines assessment/psychotherapy concepts, research synthesis, qualitative methods and ethics. The gateways precede all formally dependent courses; all offerings are checked.

blocks: Public health, health, illness & care across the lifespan

Both directly examine how biological, psychological and social factors shape health, illness and patient experience. Erasmus also integrates legal patient status and questions about health knowledge; UCR concentrates on health psychology.
Both study change across the lifecourse and older age. UCR supplies developmental psychology; Erasmus integrates care needs, ageing and social/organisational/government responses.
Health psychology and youth resilience inform service-user needs, but do not directly deliver the block’s youth-service policy, legal responsibilities, waiting lists and stakeholder project.
Healthcare systems, law, public institutions & ethics

Both examine ethical problems raised by data and technology in care. UCR explicitly discusses clinical/therapeutic confidentiality, trust and responsibility in AI; Erasmus addresses a broader set of healthcare dilemmas. This correspondence and its external credit amount remain provisional pending the regulation check.
General law and political science do not deliver the Dutch healthcare system’s institutions, financing arrangements and healthcare-specific legal framework.

Both use economic analysis of consumer/provider behaviour, market structures and intervention. UCR teaches general microeconomics; Erasmus specifically studies insurer/provider and insurance markets and their legal rules.

Both directly examine organisational structures, culture, leadership, groups and coordination. UCR supplies general organisational behaviour, while Erasmus integrates healthcare organisations, financial/logistical data and observation.

AI ethics covers an identifiable ethical part of health technology, but is more strongly aligned to Choices and Dilemmas. No included course establishes the complete healthcare innovation/business-case/implementation project.
Research methods, evidence, communication & professional practice
No scheduled course directly teaches the integrated measurement, improvement, professional regulation and quality governance of healthcare.
The credit value is unresolved: current website says 30 EC; indexed 2026–2027 OER text says 25 EC. Do not certify this retained provisional accounting value or invent an elective subject.

The external placement/independent fieldwork requirement is not delivered by the scheduled research-synthesis seminar. Optional independent research is displayed separately outside the UCR 180 EC; external credit allocation remains unverified.

notes.text: The prepared UCR programmes combine actual health and behavioural science with complementary social, economic, organisational and legal tools. They do not reproduce the Dutch healthcare system, patient law, healthcare quality/insurance framework or the required organisation-based fieldwork. The external curriculum is currently unresolved, so these prepared comparisons are withheld from presentation.

audience.programmeDescription: Health Sciences, Policy & Management of Healthcare at Erasmus studies health services through economics, law, social-medical science, public policy, organisations and ethics. Its Dutch-taught, full-time BSc combines thematic study with research and practical projects.
audience.comparisonExplanation: A reliable curriculum comparison is currently unavailable. The official sources give conflicting information about the final-year credit structure, so no complete pathway or UCR comparison is certified here.

curriculum.limitation: The programme page assigns 30 EC to free choice, while the regulation’s indexed text assigns 25 EC. The full final-year allocation and applicable requirements need confirmation from the current regulation.
